01

Mandate, data and reproducibility

A single research stack that takes a liquid US large-cap universe from raw prices to an allocation and an intrinsic-value view, with every assumption written down and every model tested rather than asserted.

The study covers 16 US large caps spread across 9 GICS sectors, benchmarked against SPY, over 2012-01-04 to 2026-09-09 — 3,691 trading days, 14.6 years. Prices are dividend- and split-adjusted; the risk-free path and the factor returns come from the Kenneth R. French data library rather than from an assumed constant.

How to read this
Every section states a finding and the test that supports it. Where a model fails, the failure is reported — a risk model nobody backtested and a Sharpe ratio without a confidence statement are both decorations. Section 8 lists what this study cannot tell you.

02

Market risk — and which risk model actually survives a backtest

Five one-day Value-at-Risk estimators are rolled forward out of sample on the Black-Litterman track record and put through the two likelihood-ratio tests the Basel traffic-light framework is built on.

At the 99% confidence level a correct model should breach on 1% of days. The normal-distribution model breaches on 2.13% — it understates the true risk by roughly 2.1× — which is the entire reason the 2008 risk-management post-mortems exist. Filtered Historical Simulation, which devolatilises returns, takes the empirical tail of the standardised residuals and re-inflates by today's conditional volatility, lands at 0.94%.

Finding
Only filtered historical achieves statistically correct unconditional coverage (Kupiec p = 0.778). Every model — including that one — still fails the independence test, meaning exceptions cluster in stress. That residual clustering is the empirical case for a GARCH filter, and it is reported here rather than hidden.

03

Is it alpha, or is it a factor you were not paid to take?

Excess return is regressed on the Fama-French five factors plus momentum with Newey-West standard errors, because daily residuals are autocorrelated and plain OLS errors routinely turn noise into a two-sigma result.

The Black-Litterman portfolio's factor regression explains 83.8% of its return variation with a market beta of 0.85. The intercept is +4.51% a year with a heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent t-statistic of 2.31.

Finding
Black-Litterman: alpha +4.51% p.a. survives factor controls (t = 2.31).

04

Portfolio construction — six allocators on one covariance matrix

The estimator, not the optimiser, is where portfolio construction usually goes wrong. Expected returns come from a Black-Litterman posterior anchored on market equilibrium; the covariance matrix is Ledoit-Wolf shrunk.

Ledoit-Wolf selects a shrinkage intensity of 0.9% on the full sample (3,691 days against 16 assets), which is the estimator correctly saying it has enough data. It matters far more inside the backtest, where each estimate uses only 756 days. The condition number falls from 46.2 to 43.6.

Black-Litterman risk aversion is not the textbook 2.5–3.0. It is derived as δ = ERP / market variance = 0.874, so the equilibrium prior reproduces the 4.5% equity risk premium used in the valuation section instead of quietly asserting a different one.

Finding
1/N is the result to beat. Equal weighting delivers a Sharpe of 1.10 at 0.44× annual turnover, against 0.70 for SPY. Every optimiser here has to justify its estimation risk against a rule that requires no estimation at all — the DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal (2009) result, reproduced out of sample.

Intrinsic value — and what the market already believes

The honest problem with a forward DCF
At a 4.2% risk-free rate and a 4.5% equity risk premium, the base case marks almost the whole universe as expensive. That is an unfalsifiable opinion, not research. Inverting the model turns it into a claim a portfolio manager can argue with.

Finding
Across these names the market is paying an implied cost of capital of 4.7%–6.7% against a 4.2% risk-free rate — an implied equity risk premium of roughly 48–247 basis points. The gap between this model and the market is a risk-premium disagreement, not an earnings disagreement. On growth, NVDA carries the most demanding expectations (49% five-year revenue CAGR required) and PG the least (0%).

Banks are valued differently, on purpose

Free cash flow to the firm has no meaning for a bank: leverage is the business and the loan book is the working capital. The two financials are valued on residual income off book equity — if ROE equals the cost of equity for ever, the bank is worth exactly book, and everything above book has to be earned.

07

What this study cannot tell you

The limitations that would materially change the conclusions, stated plainly. A research note that lists none is hiding them.

Read this before quoting any number above
The single largest bias here is universe selection. These 16 names were chosen in 2026 and are today's US large caps, so every strategy inherits the hindsight of picking companies that survived and compounded. The absolute returns are therefore not investable alpha. What remains valid is the relative comparison: every allocator faces the identical universe, calendar, costs and constraints, so the ranking between them is a fair test even though the level is not.
  • Survivorship and selection. No delisted or acquired names, and no point-in-time index membership. Treat cross-strategy differences as the result; treat the level of returns as an upper bound.
  • Single market, single currency. US large-cap equity only. No credit, no rates, no FX, no small caps, no non-US listings — so the correlation structure is far friendlier than a real book's.
  • Long-only, fully invested. No shorting, no leverage, no cash allocation and no derivatives overlay, which removes most of the ways a real mandate can go wrong.
  • {cfg['backtest']['transaction_cost_bps']:.0f}bp on traded notional. Real costs are state-dependent and rise exactly when a strategy wants to trade most; market impact and borrow are not modelled at all.
  • The valuation inputs are the modeller's estimates, not a fundamentals feed. They are versioned in config/fundamentals.yaml so they can be re-keyed from filings and the whole report regenerated — that is the mitigation, not a claim that they are audited.
  • Factor data lags prices by several weeks; factor statistics use the overlapping window only, so the most recent period is absent from the attribution but present in the performance figures.
  • Multiple testing. Several strategies were evaluated on one sample. The Deflated Sharpe p-value in section 5 is the correction; it is reported for every strategy, not only the flattering ones.
  • Nothing here is investment advice, a price target, or a recommendation. It is a demonstration of method.
08

Method and reproducibility

How to regenerate every number in this document.

  • Data. Daily adjusted closes from the public Yahoo Finance chart endpoint, cached to data/raw/prices/ and committed. Factor and risk-free series from the Kenneth R. French Data Library, cached to data/raw/factors/. The repository reproduces offline.
  • Alignment. Prices, factors and the risk-free path are joined once in ResearchPanel. The market calendar is authoritative.
  • Estimation. Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage for covariance; Black-Litterman for expected returns; Newey-West for regression inference.
  • Backtest. Point-in-time loop, drift between rebalances, costs on traded notional. Allocators receive a StrategyContext that carries only data available at the rebalance date.
  • Valuation. Two-stage FCFF with mid-year discounting and steady-state reinvestment; residual income for banks; Monte Carlo and Brent-solved reverse DCF on top.
  • Tests. pytest covers the analytics against closed-form results, the optimisers against their defining properties (equal risk contribution, budget constraints), the vectorised Monte Carlo against the pandas DCF, and the backtest against look-ahead.
  • Run it. make install && make data && make pipeline, or quantdesk run.

Reproducibility. Every figure and table in this document is generated by <code>quantdesk run</code> from the committed data cache and the two YAML configuration files. There are no hand-entered numbers in the report.

Disclaimer. This document is a demonstration of quantitative research method. It is not investment advice, not a recommendation, and not a price target. The valuation inputs are the author's own normalised estimates and must be re-keyed from primary filings before any decision is taken.
